chapter_title: Organic Chemistry Name Reactions: Complete Exam & Mechanism Guide

notes_list.title: What is a Name Reaction?
notes_list.basic_overview: A name reaction is an organic transformation traditionally associated with a particular chemist or commonly recognized name. For examinations, the reaction name must be connected with substrate, reagent, conditions, major product and mechanism.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam rule: Do not memorize only the reagent. Build the chain: substrate class → reagent/condition → reaction type → product → mechanism → selectivity. Example: Aldehyde/ketone + Zn(Hg)/HCl → hydrocarbon is Clemmensen reduction, whereas aldehyde/ketone + NH2NH2/KOH, heat → hydrocarbon is Wolff–Kishner reduction.

notes_list.title: Four Things to Identify in Every Name Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: For every named reaction identify the starting functional group, key reagent, bond-forming or bond-breaking event and characteristic product.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A useful revision table should contain: Reaction name | substrate | reagent | conditions | product | mechanism | important limitation. This format is especially useful for GATE, CSIR-NET, MSc entrance and PSU examinations.

notes_list.title: Name Reaction vs Named Reagent
notes_list.basic_overview: A named reagent and a name reaction are not identical. A reagent may participate in several transformations, while a name reaction describes a characteristic transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: PCC is a named reagent used for oxidation, but PCC oxidation itself is not always treated as a single universally defined name reaction. In contrast, Cannizzaro, Aldol, Claisen and Diels–Alder describe characteristic reaction patterns.

notes_list.title: Aldol Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones containing an alpha-hydrogen can undergo base- or acid-catalysed condensation to form a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, which may dehydrate to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 2 CH3CHO --dilute NaOH→ CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO; on heating/dehydration → CH3CH=CHCHO. Mechanistically, base generates an enolate, the enolate attacks another carbonyl compound, protonation gives the beta-hydroxy product and dehydration gives the conjugated alkene. Exam trap: aldehydes/ketones without alpha-H cannot undergo the normal self-aldol pathway.

notes_list.title: Crossed Aldol Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: A crossed aldol reaction occurs between two different carbonyl compounds. Selectivity is easier when one partner forms the nucleophilic enolate while the other partner lacks alpha-hydrogen.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Benzaldehyde lacks alpha-H and therefore commonly acts as the electrophilic carbonyl partner in crossed aldol reactions with acetone or acetophenone derivatives. Multiple products may occur when both reactants possess alpha-H.

notes_list.title: Claisen Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: An ester containing an alpha-hydrogen reacts with a suitable alkoxide base to form a beta-keto ester through carbon–carbon bond formation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General pattern: 2 RCH2COOR' --RO−/ROH→ RCOCH2CH2COOR' followed by formation of the beta-keto ester framework. The alkoxide base is generally chosen to match the ester alkoxy group to minimize transesterification. A final acidic work-up protonates the enolate.

notes_list.title: Dieckmann Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: Dieckmann condensation is the intramolecular version of the Claisen condensation and commonly produces cyclic beta-keto esters.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction is especially favorable for formation of five- and six-membered rings. Exam strategy: identify a diester containing an alpha-H and check whether intramolecular attack can create a favorable ring.

notes_list.title: Perkin Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: An aromatic aldehyde reacts with an acid anhydride in the presence of the corresponding carboxylate base to produce an alpha,beta-unsaturated aromatic carboxylic acid after work-up.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Classical example: benzaldehyde + acetic anhydride/sodium acetate → cinnamic acid after hydrolysis. The anhydride-derived enolate attacks the aromatic aldehyde followed by elimination and hydrolysis.

notes_list.title: Knoevenagel Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones react with active methylene compounds such as malonates, malononitrile or beta-dicarbonyl compounds under basic or amine catalysis to form alkenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The active methylene compound is sufficiently acidic because its conjugate base is stabilized by electron-withdrawing groups. The reaction commonly gives a conjugated alkene. Exam clue: carbonyl + CH2 flanked by strong electron-withdrawing groups.

notes_list.title: Benzoin Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: Two aromatic aldehydes can undergo coupling to form an alpha-hydroxy ketone known as benzoin. Cyanide ion or thiamine-derived catalysts can facilitate the transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Classical reaction: 2 PhCHO --CN−→ PhCH(OH)COPh. Cyanide acts through polarity reversal (umpolung) of the aldehyde carbonyl carbon, allowing carbon–carbon bond formation between two aldehyde molecules.

notes_list.title: Grignard Addition
notes_list.basic_overview: Grignard reagents RMgX behave as carbon nucleophiles and add to aldehydes and ketones. Acidic work-up converts the resulting alkoxide into an alcohol.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RMgX + formaldehyde → primary alcohol; RMgX + aldehyde other than formaldehyde → secondary alcohol; RMgX + ketone → tertiary alcohol. Water, alcohols, acids and other proton donors destroy Grignard reagents, so reactions require dry ether or THF-type conditions.

notes_list.title: Grignard with Esters
notes_list.basic_overview: Esters generally react with two equivalents of Grignard reagent to give tertiary alcohols after hydrolysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content: First addition gives a tetrahedral intermediate followed by loss of alkoxide and formation of a ketone. The ketone reacts rapidly with a second equivalent of Grignard reagent, ultimately giving a tertiary alcohol.

notes_list.title: Wittig Olefination
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones react with phosphorus ylides to replace the carbonyl oxygen with a carbon substituent and form an alkene.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General transformation: R2C=O + Ph3P=CHR → R2C=CHR + Ph3P=O. The strong formation of P=O drives the reaction. Exam clue: carbonyl compound + phosphonium ylide → alkene.

notes_list.title: Corey–Fuchs Homologation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes can be converted into terminal alkynes through conversion to a gem-dibromoalkene followed by organolithium-mediated transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical sequence: aldehyde → gem-dibromoalkene using CBr4/PPh3-type conditions → terminal alkyne using strong base such as n-BuLi. The reaction is useful for extending carbon skeletons with an alkyne terminus.

notes_list.title: Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl or vinyl halides/triflates react with organoboron compounds in the presence of a palladium catalyst and base to form C–C bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General pattern: Ar–X + Ar'–B(OH)2 --Pd/base→ Ar–Ar'. The catalytic cycle involves oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive elimination. Suzuki coupling is valued for functional-group tolerance and the relatively convenient handling of organoboron reagents.

notes_list.title: Mizoroki–Heck Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: An aryl or vinyl halide reacts with an alkene under palladium catalysis and base to form a substituted alkene.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Key catalytic steps include oxidative addition of the aryl halide, alkene coordination and migratory insertion, beta-hydride elimination and catalyst regeneration. Regioselectivity often favors the more substituted alkene arrangement, but substrate and catalyst conditions matter.

notes_list.title: Sonogashira Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl or vinyl halides react with terminal alkynes under palladium catalysis, often with a copper co-catalyst or copper-free variants, to form C(sp2)–C(sp) bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam clue: aryl halide + terminal alkyne + Pd catalyst → aryl alkyne. The terminal alkyne is deprotonated and transferred to the palladium catalytic system before reductive elimination.

notes_list.title: Negishi Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organozinc reagents couple with organic halides or related electrophiles under transition-metal catalysis to form carbon–carbon bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The organozinc reagent participates in transmetalation after oxidative addition of the electrophile to the metal catalyst, followed by reductive elimination.

notes_list.title: Kumada Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Grignard reagents react with aryl or vinyl halides under nickel or palladium catalysis to form carbon–carbon bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam clue: organomagnesium reagent + aryl/vinyl halide + Ni/Pd → coupled product. Grignard reagents are highly reactive, so functional-group compatibility can be lower than with milder organoboron reagents.

notes_list.title: Baeyer–Villiger Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Ketones are converted into esters using peroxy acids or related oxidants. Cyclic ketones give lactones.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The oxygen inserted between carbonyl carbon and one substituent. Migratory aptitude is important: groups with greater ability to stabilize positive charge generally migrate more readily. Aldehydes can give formate-related products under suitable conditions.

notes_list.title: Ozonolysis of Alkenes
notes_list.basic_overview: Ozone cleaves carbon–carbon double bonds. Reductive work-up commonly gives aldehydes and ketones, whereas oxidative work-up can convert aldehyde-derived fragments further to carboxylic acids.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Structural clue: replace the C=C bond by carbonyl groups. For CH3CH=CHCH3, reductive ozonolysis gives two CH3CHO molecules. Ozonolysis is widely used for locating alkene positions.

notes_list.title: OsO4 Dihydroxylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes can be converted into vicinal cis-diols through osmium tetroxide-mediated syn dihydroxylation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: OsO4 adds to both alkene carbons from the same face, leading to syn addition. Catalytic OsO4 can be regenerated using a co-oxidant such as NMO or H2O2.

notes_list.title: Sharpless Epoxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Enantioselective epoxidation of suitable allylic alcohols is achieved using titanium alkoxide, a chiral tartrate and an oxidant such as tert-butyl hydroperoxide.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction is important because the chiral catalyst system controls which enantiomeric epoxide is preferentially formed. The standard mnemonic uses the orientation of the allylic alcohol and the selected tartrate enantiomer to predict product configuration.

notes_list.title: Wacker Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Terminal alkenes can be oxidized to methyl ketones under palladium(II)-catalysed oxidative conditions, commonly involving PdCl2 and a copper/oxygen regeneration system.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For a simple terminal alkene RCH=CH2, the usual Wacker product is RCOCH3. The reaction proceeds through alkene coordination, nucleophilic water addition and oxidation-related steps.

notes_list.title: Swern Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes and ketones, respectively, under mild, anhydrous conditions using activated DMSO and a suitable activating agent such as oxalyl chloride.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Swern oxidation avoids heavy-metal oxidants and is useful for sensitive substrates. Low temperature is commonly used during activation and alcohol addition. Dimethyl sulfide is produced as a characteristic by-product.

topics.basic_overview: Aldehydes can be selectively oxidized to carboxylic acids using sodium chlorite under controlled conditions.
topics.extra_info_content: Pinnick oxidation is particularly useful when mild and selective aldehyde-to-acid conversion is needed. Scavengers such as sulfamic acid or related additives may be used to manage chlorite-derived side products.

notes_list.title: Clemmensen Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to hydrocarbons using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid under strongly acidic conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General transformation: R2C=O → R2CH2. Key exam distinction: Clemmensen is strongly acidic, whereas Wolff–Kishner reduction is strongly basic. Choose based on whether the molecule is stable under acidic or basic conditions.

notes_list.title: Wolff–Kishner Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones are converted into hydrocarbons through hydrazone formation followed by strongly basic heating.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical conditions involve hydrazine or a substituted hydrazine and strong base such as KOH with heat. Exam comparison: Clemmensen = acidic; Wolff–Kishner = basic.

notes_list.title: Birch Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings are partially reduced to nonconjugated or cyclohexadiene-type products using an alkali metal, liquid ammonia and an alcohol proton source.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction produces a 1,4-diene system. Substituent effects influence which carbon atoms retain the double bonds. Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents affect regiochemistry differently, making substituent analysis important for advanced exam problems.

notes_list.title: Luche Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Sodium borohydride in the presence of cerium(III) salts, commonly CeCl3, provides enhanced selective reduction of carbonyl compounds, especially aldehydes and ketones in suitable systems.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A common exam concept is chemoselectivity: NaBH4/CeCl3 can favor carbonyl reduction while avoiding some competing reactions that stronger hydride reagents might cause.

notes_list.title: Rosenmund Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Acid chlorides are selectively reduced to aldehydes using hydrogen gas over poisoned palladium catalyst.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical catalyst: Pd/BaSO4, often modified or poisoned to reduce over-reduction of the aldehyde. General transformation: RCOCl → RCHO.

notes_list.title: Friedel–Crafts Alkylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings react with suitable alkylating agents in the presence of Lewis acids such as AlCl3 to introduce an alkyl group.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Classical example: benzene + CH3Cl/AlCl3 → toluene. Limitations include carbocation rearrangements, polyalkylation and failure with strongly deactivated aromatic rings. Friedel–Crafts alkylation is generally unsuitable for strongly electron-withdrawing substituents.

notes_list.title: Friedel–Crafts Acylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings react with acyl chlorides or acid anhydrides in the presence of Lewis acids to form aryl ketones.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The electrophile is an acylium ion, RCO+. Because the acylium ion is resonance stabilized, rearrangement is normally avoided. Acylation usually stops after monoacylation because the acyl group deactivates the ring.

notes_list.title: Reimer–Tiemann Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Phenols can be converted into mainly ortho-hydroxy aromatic aldehydes using chloroform and strong base.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction generates dichlorocarbene from CHCl3 under strongly basic conditions. Phenoxide directs electrophilic substitution predominantly to the ortho position. Salicylaldehyde is a classical major product from phenol.

notes_list.title: Kolbe–Schmitt Carboxylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Sodium phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide under pressure and heat to form salicylate, which gives salicylic acid after acidification.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The transformation introduces CO2-derived carbon at the ortho position relative to oxygen. Industrially relevant conditions use elevated pressure and temperature. Exam clue: phenoxide + CO2 → salicylic acid after acidification.

notes_list.title: Gattermann–Koch Formylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic compounds can be formylated using carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in the presence of Lewis-acid systems such as AlCl3/CuCl.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction introduces a formyl group directly onto an activated aromatic ring. It is an electrophilic aromatic substitution process involving a formyl electrophile equivalent.

notes_list.title: Gattermann Formylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic diazonium salts can be converted into aromatic aldehydes under conditions involving HCN/HCl and a Lewis-acid catalyst in the classical formylation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Do not confuse Gattermann formylation of diazonium compounds with Gattermann–Koch formylation of aromatic hydrocarbons using CO/HCl.

notes_list.title: Sandmeyer Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl diazonium salts are converted into aryl chlorides, bromides or nitriles using copper(I) salts such as CuCl, CuBr or CuCN.
notes_list.extra_info_content: ArN2+ can be replaced by Cl, Br or CN. Example: aniline → diazonium salt → chlorobenzene using CuCl. Nitrogen gas leaves during the transformation.

notes_list.title: Balz–Schiemann Fluorination
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl diazonium tetrafluoroborate salts decompose on heating to produce aryl fluorides with loss of nitrogen and boron-containing products.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam clue: ArN2+BF4− --heat→ ArF + N2 + BF3-related products. This is a classical method for replacing an aromatic diazonium group with fluorine.

notes_list.title: Hunsdiecker Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Silver salts of carboxylic acids undergo oxidative decarboxylative halogenation to produce alkyl halides with one fewer carbon atom.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General pattern: RCOOAg + Br2/light → RBr + CO2 + AgBr. The carbon skeleton loses the carboxyl carbon. This one-carbon shortening is a common examination clue.

notes_list.title: Williamson Ether Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: An alkoxide ion reacts with an alkyl halide or sulfonate through an SN2 pathway to form an ether.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Best substrates for the electrophile are primary alkyl halides. Secondary substrates may compete with elimination, while tertiary alkyl halides generally favor elimination rather than clean SN2 substitution. Example: CH3CH2ONa + CH3I → CH3CH2OCH3.

notes_list.title: Pinacol–Pinacolone Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Vicinal diols undergo acid-catalysed rearrangement to carbonyl compounds through loss of water followed by migration.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction involves protonation of an OH group, water loss, carbocation formation and 1,2-migration with carbonyl formation. Migratory aptitude and carbocation stability influence product formation.

notes_list.title: Cumene Process
notes_list.basic_overview: Cumene is oxidized to cumene hydroperoxide, which undergoes acid-catalysed cleavage to produce phenol and acetone.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Industrial significance: benzene + propene → cumene; oxidation → cumene hydroperoxide; acid cleavage → phenol + acetone. Exam clue: major industrial route to phenol.

notes_list.title: Hydroboration–Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes react with borane or substituted boranes followed by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide under basic conditions to give alcohols with overall anti-Markovnikov hydration.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The H and B atoms add syn across the double bond, with boron generally attaching to the less substituted carbon. Oxidation replaces the C–B bond with C–O without changing the carbon framework. Overall result: anti-Markovnikov alcohol with syn addition in the hydroboration step.

notes_list.title: Oxymercuration–Demercuration
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes are converted into Markovnikov alcohols without the carbocation rearrangements characteristic of simple acid-catalysed hydration.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical sequence: alkene + Hg(OAc)2/H2O followed by NaBH4. The mercurinium ion intermediate controls regioselectivity, while the final demercuration replaces the C–Hg group with hydrogen.

notes_list.title: Kharasch Effect
notes_list.basic_overview: In the presence of peroxides, HBr can add to an alkene through a radical chain mechanism to give the anti-Markovnikov product.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The peroxide effect is characteristic of HBr in the classical exam context. HCl and HI do not normally give the same useful anti-Markovnikov radical addition because of unfavorable energetics of the propagation steps.

notes_list.title: Lindlar Catalyst Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkynes are selectively hydrogenated to cis-alkenes using a poisoned palladium catalyst known as Lindlar catalyst.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The catalyst is deliberately deactivated so that hydrogenation stops at the alkene stage. Syn addition of hydrogen gives the cis-alkene. Exam comparison: Lindlar → cis-alkene; dissolving-metal reduction such as Na/NH3(l) → trans-alkene.

notes_list.title: Na/NH3 Reduction of Alkynes
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkynes are reduced to trans-alkenes under dissolving-metal conditions such as sodium or lithium in liquid ammonia.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The mechanism proceeds through radical-anion and protonation steps, leading to anti addition overall. Exam clue: alkyne → trans-alkene.

notes_list.title: Diels–Alder Cycloaddition
notes_list.basic_overview: A conjugated diene reacts with an alkene or alkyne dienophile through a thermal [4+2] cycloaddition to form a six-membered ring.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction is stereospecific and concerted. The diene generally needs an s-cis conformation. Electron-withdrawing groups on the dienophile usually increase reactivity, while electron-donating groups on the diene can increase reactivity. The endo product is often kinetically favored with suitable substituents.

notes_list.title: Claisen Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Allyl vinyl ethers undergo a thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to form gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compounds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The rearrangement is concerted and proceeds through a six-membered transition-state arrangement. Bond connectivity changes without ionic intermediates. Stereochemical information can be transferred predictably through the cyclic transition state.

notes_list.title: Cope Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: A 1,5-diene undergoes a thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to another 1,5-diene.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction proceeds through a six-membered cyclic transition state. Chair-like transition states are often favored when steric interactions are minimized.

notes_list.title: Electrocyclic Ring Opening and Closing
notes_list.basic_overview: Conjugated polyenes undergo reversible ring opening or ring closure through electrocyclic reactions whose stereochemical mode depends on the number of pi electrons and thermal or photochemical conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Woodward–Hoffmann rules: under thermal conditions, systems with 4n pi electrons undergo conrotatory electrocyclization, while systems with 4n+2 pi electrons undergo disrotatory electrocyclization. Photochemical conditions reverse these preferences.

notes_list.title: Beckmann Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Oximes undergo acid-promoted rearrangement to amides. Cyclic ketoximes can produce lactams.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The group anti to the leaving group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as water or another leaving group departs. Therefore stereochemical configuration of the oxime is important. Exam clue: ketoxime → amide; cyclic ketoxime → lactam.

notes_list.title: Baeyer–Villiger Migratory Aptitude
notes_list.basic_overview: In Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, one group adjacent to the carbonyl migrates to oxygen while the carbonyl compound is converted into an ester or lactone.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical migratory aptitude trends depend on substrate and conditions; groups better able to stabilize positive charge in the transition state generally migrate more readily. Hydride and tertiary-type migration can be highly favorable in appropriate substrates.

notes_list.title: Favorskii Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Alpha-halo ketones undergo base-induced rearrangement to carboxylic acid derivatives, often producing ring-contracted products when cyclic substrates are used.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The mechanism is commonly described through a cyclopropanone-related intermediate or equivalent pathway depending on substrate and conditions. A key exam clue is alpha-halo ketone + base → rearranged carboxylate/ester/amide derivative.

notes_list.title: Hofmann Bromamide Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary amides are converted into primary amines containing one fewer carbon atom using bromine and strong base or related hypohalite conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General transformation: RCONH2 → RNH2 + CO2-derived products. The carbonyl carbon is lost. Mechanistically, the amide is converted into an isocyanate intermediate, which undergoes hydrolysis to the amine.

notes_list.title: Curtius Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Acyl azides undergo thermal rearrangement to isocyanates, which can be hydrolysed to primary amines or trapped by alcohols to form carbamates.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RCO2H can first be converted to an activated derivative and then acyl azide; heating gives RNCO. The migrating group moves from carbonyl carbon to nitrogen during nitrogen extrusion. Like Hofmann rearrangement, the final amine has one fewer carbon than the original carboxylic acid framework.

notes_list.title: Schmidt Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids and ketones can undergo acid-mediated reactions with hydrazoic acid, giving nitrogen-containing products through migration and nitrogen extrusion.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For carboxylic acids, the rearrangement can produce isocyanates that lead to amines after hydrolysis. For cyclic ketones, ring-expanded lactams can form.

notes_list.title: Cannizzaro Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes without alpha-hydrogen undergo base-induced disproportionation to produce an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 2 PhCHO + OH− → PhCH2OH + PhCOO−. One aldehyde molecule is oxidized and another is reduced. Exam clue: non-enolizable aldehyde + concentrated base.

notes_list.title: Crossed Cannizzaro Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Two different aldehydes without alpha-hydrogen can undergo crossed Cannizzaro reaction, often designed so that one aldehyde acts preferentially as the reducing partner.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Formaldehyde is particularly effective as the aldehyde that is oxidized to formate while another non-enolizable aldehyde is reduced to its alcohol. This selectivity is frequently tested.

notes_list.title: Haloform Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Methyl ketones and suitable secondary alcohols are oxidatively cleaved under halogen/base conditions to produce carboxylate and haloform.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Iodoform test uses I2/NaOH and gives yellow CHI3 precipitate for methyl ketones and compounds that can be oxidized to methyl ketones, such as ethanol and suitable secondary alcohols containing CH3CH(OH)−.

notes_list.title: Baeyer Test for Unsaturation
notes_list.basic_overview: Cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate is classically used as a qualitative test for readily oxidizable unsaturation, producing loss of purple permanganate color and formation of manganese dioxide under typical conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: This is a qualitative test rather than a definitive structural proof because other reducing or oxidizable substances can also react with permanganate.

notes_list.title: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids containing alpha-hydrogen undergo alpha-halogenation using halogen and phosphorus-based reagents, commonly Br2/PBr3-type conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The carboxylic acid is first converted into an acyl halide, which can enolize and undergo alpha-halogenation. Hydrolysis regenerates the carboxylic acid. Exam clue: carboxylic acid + alpha-H → alpha-halo acid.

notes_list.title: Malonic Ester Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Diethyl malonate is deprotonated at the active methylene carbon, alkylated with suitable alkyl halides and then hydrolysed and decarboxylated to synthesize substituted acetic acids.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General route: CH2(CO2Et)2 → alkylation → hydrolysis → heating/decarboxylation → RCH2CO2H. Primary alkyl halides are generally preferred for clean SN2 alkylation.

notes_list.title: Acetoacetic Ester Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Ethyl acetoacetate is alkylated at its active methylene carbon, followed by hydrolysis and decarboxylation to synthesize substituted methyl ketones.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General sequence: ethyl acetoacetate → enolate formation → alkylation → hydrolysis → decarboxylation → substituted methyl ketone. This is a major retrosynthetic strategy for building ketones.

notes_list.title: Arndt–Eistert Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids can be converted into homologated acids containing one additional carbon through an acid chloride → diazoketone → ketene sequence followed by trapping with water or another nucleophile.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Classical sequence: RCOOH → RCOCl → RCOCHN2 → ketene → RCH2COOH. The carbon count increases by one in the final carboxylic acid.

notes_list.title: Gabriel Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Potassium phthalimide reacts with suitable primary alkyl halides through SN2 substitution and subsequent cleavage gives primary amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The method is especially useful for preparing primary amines without the multiple alkylation often associated with direct ammonia alkylation. It is poorly suited to tertiary alkyl halides because SN2 substitution is unfavorable.

notes_list.title: Hofmann Mustard Oil Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary amines react with carbon disulfide and subsequent reagents to produce isothiocyanates, commonly recognized through the mustard-oil reaction.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Primary amines can be converted to isothiocyanates, R–N=C=S, which have characteristic pungent mustard-oil odors. The reaction is mainly of qualitative and historical significance in organic identification.

notes_list.title: Carbylamine Test
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary amines react with chloroform and alcoholic KOH on heating to form isocyanides with a characteristic unpleasant odor.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Only primary amines give the classical carbylamine test. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this reaction under the standard test conditions. General product: RNH2 → RNC.

notes_list.title: Hofmann Elimination
notes_list.basic_overview: Quaternary ammonium hydroxides undergo elimination on heating to form alkenes. The major alkene is often the less substituted alkene, known as the Hofmann product.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The bulky leaving group and steric factors contribute to preference for abstraction of the most accessible beta-hydrogen. This can oppose the usual Zaitsev orientation observed in many ordinary elimination reactions.

notes_list.title: Bischler–Möhlau Indole Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Anilines react with alpha-haloketones under suitable conditions to form substituted indoles.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reaction constructs the indole framework through condensation and cyclization processes. It is useful in heterocyclic synthesis and can appear in advanced MSc, GATE and CSIR-NET questions.

notes_list.title: Fischer Indole Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl hydrazines react with aldehydes or ketones under acidic conditions to form indoles.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The carbonyl compound first forms an arylhydrazone, followed by acid-catalysed rearrangement and cyclization to the indole framework. Fischer indole synthesis is one of the most important named methods for constructing indoles.

notes_list.title: Paal–Knorr Pyrrole Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds can cyclize to pyrroles under suitable acid-promoted conditions with ammonia or primary amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Variants of the Paal–Knorr strategy also provide furans and thiophenes depending on the heteroatom source. Exam clue: 1,4-dicarbonyl → five-membered heterocycle.

notes_list.title: Hantzsch Pyridine Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Beta-ketoesters, an aldehyde and ammonia or an ammonium source undergo multicomponent condensation to produce substituted 1,4-dihydropyridines, which can be oxidized to pyridines.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Hantzsch synthesis is a classic multicomponent heterocycle-forming reaction. Oxidation of the dihydropyridine product provides an aromatic pyridine derivative.

notes_list.title: Gewald Thiophene Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: A carbonyl compound, an activated nitrile and sulfur undergo base-promoted condensation and cyclization to form substituted 2-aminothiophenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam clue: carbonyl compound + activated nitrile + sulfur → 2-aminothiophene framework. The reaction is important for medicinal and heterocyclic chemistry.

notes_list.title: Boc Protection of Amines
notes_list.basic_overview: Amines can be protected as carbamates using di-tert-butyl dicarbonate, commonly written as Boc2O.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Boc protection converts RNH2 into RNHBoc. The Boc group is commonly removed under acidic conditions such as TFA or HCl in suitable solvents. Exam clue: Boc is acid-labile.

notes_list.title: Cbz Protection
notes_list.basic_overview: Amines can be protected as carbamates using benzyl chloroformate (Cbz-Cl).
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cbz-protected amines are commonly deprotected by catalytic hydrogenolysis, for example H2/Pd-C. Exam contrast: Boc is commonly acid-labile, whereas Cbz is commonly removed by hydrogenolysis.

notes_list.title: Carbonyl Protection as Acetal
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones can be protected as acetals or ketals by reaction with alcohols under acid catalysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Acetal formation is reversible and generally requires removal of water to drive formation. Acetals are stable under many basic conditions and are commonly hydrolysed under aqueous acidic conditions to regenerate the carbonyl.

notes_list.title: THP Protection of Alcohols
notes_list.basic_overview: Alcohols can be protected as tetrahydropyranyl ethers using dihydropyran under acid catalysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content: THP ethers are commonly stable to many bases and can be removed under acidic hydrolysis conditions. The THP group is useful when a temporary acid-sensitive protection strategy is not appropriate.

sections.title: Important Named Reagents & Their Signature Transformations

notes_list.title: PCC Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Pyridinium chlorochromate commonly oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones under anhydrous conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam clue: primary alcohol + PCC → aldehyde under controlled anhydrous conditions. Stronger aqueous chromium(VI) oxidation can continue primary alcohol oxidation to carboxylic acid.

notes_list.title: DIBAL-H Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: DIBAL-H can selectively reduce esters and nitriles to aldehydes under controlled low-temperature conditions, although exact selectivity depends on substrate and stoichiometry.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A common exam transformation is ester → aldehyde using approximately controlled DIBAL-H conditions. Excess or warmer conditions can lead to further reduction.

notes_list.title: mCPBA Epoxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: m-Chloroperoxybenzoic acid is commonly used to convert alkenes into epoxides.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The oxygen transfer is stereospecific: alkene geometry is retained in the relative configuration of substituents in the epoxide. mCPBA can also participate in Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of suitable ketones.

notes_list.title: NBS Allylic and Benzylic Bromination
notes_list.basic_overview: N-Bromosuccinimide is commonly used as a controlled source of low concentrations of bromine for radical allylic and benzylic bromination.
notes_list.extra_info_content: NBS maintains a low bromine concentration, favoring radical substitution at allylic or benzylic positions under radical initiation conditions. Exam clue: alkene + NBS/hν → allylic bromination rather than simple addition of Br2.

topics.title: LiAlH4
topics.basic_overview: Lithium aluminium hydride is a strong hydride reducing agent capable of reducing many carboxylic acid derivatives, aldehydes and ketones to alcohols or related reduced products.
topics.extra_info_content: LiAlH4 reacts violently with water and protic solvents and is normally used under anhydrous conditions followed by careful work-up. Common exam transformations: carboxylic acid → primary alcohol; ester → primary alcohols; amide → amine.

topics.title: NaBH4
topics.basic_overview: Sodium borohydride is a milder hydride reagent that commonly reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols under suitable conditions.
topics.extra_info_content: Compared with LiAlH4, NaBH4 is generally more chemoselective for aldehydes and ketones and is compatible with many protic solvents under appropriate conditions.

sections.title: Advanced Cross-Coupling & Modern C–C/C–N Bond Formation

notes_list.title: Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl halides or related electrophiles react with amines under palladium catalysis and suitable ligand/base systems to form aryl amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The catalytic cycle commonly involves oxidative addition, amine coordination/deprotonation, reductive elimination and catalyst regeneration. Ligand choice strongly influences reactivity and selectivity.

notes_list.title: Ullmann Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Copper-mediated coupling of aryl halides can form biaryls or aryl heteroatom bonds depending on the nucleophile and reaction conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Classical Ullmann biaryl coupling uses copper and heat. Modern copper-catalysed variants can form C–N, C–O and C–S bonds under more controlled conditions.

notes_list.title: Hiyama Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organosilicon compounds can couple with aryl or vinyl halides under palladium catalysis, often requiring activation by fluoride or base.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General pattern: organosilane + aryl/vinyl halide → coupled product. The reaction is useful because organosilicon reagents can be relatively stable and convenient to handle.

notes_list.title: Stille Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organotin reagents couple with organic halides under palladium catalysis to form C–C bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content: General pattern: R–SnR3 + Ar–X --Pd→ R–Ar. The reaction is broadly useful but organotin reagent toxicity and waste are important practical disadvantages.

sections.title: Name Reactions with Important Stereochemical Outcomes

notes_list.title: Reactions Giving Syn Addition
notes_list.basic_overview: Hydroboration and catalytic hydrogenation commonly involve syn addition of the two newly introduced atoms or groups across a pi bond.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Hydroboration–oxidation: H and OH have an overall syn relationship in the appropriate stereochemical description. Lindlar reduction: H2 adds syn to an alkyne to give a cis-alkene.

notes_list.title: Reactions Giving Anti Addition
notes_list.basic_overview: Bromination of alkenes through a bromonium ion commonly gives anti addition, and dissolving-metal reduction of alkynes gives an overall anti addition of hydrogen.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Bromonium-ion formation blocks attack from the same face, favoring backside opening. Na/NH3 reduction of alkynes gives trans-alkenes through a radical-anion pathway.

notes_list.title: Regioselectivity Map
notes_list.basic_overview: Markovnikov orientation commonly places H on the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms and the other group on the more substituted carbon. Hydroboration–oxidation gives the opposite regioselectivity.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Important examples: alkene + HBr under ordinary ionic conditions → Markovnikov; alkene + HBr/peroxide → anti-Markovnikov radical addition; hydroboration–oxidation → anti-Markovnikov alcohol; oxymercuration–demercuration → Markovnikov alcohol.

notes_list.title: Clemmensen vs Wolff–Kishner
notes_list.basic_overview: Both reactions convert aldehydes and ketones to hydrocarbons, but they operate under fundamentally different conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Clemmensen: Zn(Hg)/HCl, strongly acidic. Wolff–Kishner: hydrazine/base/heat, strongly basic. Choose according to functional-group stability elsewhere in the molecule.

notes_list.title: Cis vs Trans Alkene from Alkyne
notes_list.basic_overview: Partial reduction of alkynes can be controlled to produce either cis- or trans-alkenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Lindlar catalyst + H2 → cis-alkene. Na/NH3(l) or Li/NH3(l) → trans-alkene. Complete catalytic hydrogenation with excess H2 can continue to the alkane.

notes_list.title: Diazonium Replacement Comparison
notes_list.basic_overview: Both reactions use aryl diazonium chemistry, but their reagent systems and introduced groups differ.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Sandmeyer: CuCl/CuBr/CuCN can replace diazonium by Cl, Br or CN. Balz–Schiemann: diazonium tetrafluoroborate gives aryl fluoride on heating.

notes_list.title: Friedel–Crafts Comparison
notes_list.basic_overview: Both are electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions catalysed by Lewis acids, but one installs an alkyl group and the other an acyl group.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Alkylation: alkyl electrophile, possible rearrangement and polyalkylation. Acylation: acylium ion, generally no carbocation rearrangement and usually monoacylation because the ring becomes deactivated by the acyl group.

notes_list.title: Synthesis Strategy Comparison
notes_list.basic_overview: Both syntheses use active methylene compounds followed by alkylation, hydrolysis and decarboxylation, but their final carbonyl products differ.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Malonic ester synthesis → substituted acetic acid derivatives. Acetoacetic ester synthesis → substituted methyl ketones. This distinction is a common retrosynthesis and MCQ question.

topics.topic_title: Wrong Product Due to Missing Alpha Hydrogen

notes_list.title: Check Alpha-H Before Aldol
notes_list.basic_overview: Before predicting an aldol reaction, determine whether the carbonyl compound has at least one alpha-hydrogen capable of enolate formation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: If a carbonyl compound lacks alpha-H, ordinary self-aldol chemistry is not available. Benzaldehyde is the classic example. Under strong base it can instead undergo Cannizzaro reaction.

topics.topic_title: Wrong Grignard Product Due to Proton Source

notes_list.title: Check for Acidic Proton
notes_list.basic_overview: Grignard reagents are strong bases as well as nucleophiles and are quenched by compounds containing sufficiently acidic protons.
notes_list.extra_info_content: OH, NH, SH and COOH groups can consume RMgX before the desired carbonyl addition occurs. Protect or otherwise manage such functional groups when necessary.

notes_list.title: Carbocation Rearrangement Check
notes_list.basic_overview: Friedel–Crafts alkylation can involve carbocation-like electrophiles, so hydride or alkyl shifts may change the final carbon skeleton.
notes_list.extra_info_content: When predicting a product, draw the most stable carbocation or carbocation-like intermediate before aromatic attack. Friedel–Crafts acylation avoids this particular rearrangement issue because the acylium ion is resonance stabilized.

topics.topic_title: SN2 Failure in Williamson Ether Synthesis

notes_list.title: Check Electrophile Structure
notes_list.basic_overview: Williamson ether synthesis works best with unhindered primary electrophiles because it proceeds through SN2 substitution.
notes_list.extra_info_content: If the electrophile is tertiary, strong base and heat can favor elimination. For secondary substrates, substitution and elimination may compete. Redesign the synthesis so the alkoxide attacks a primary alkyl electrophile whenever possible.

topics.topic_title: Using Ozonolysis to Locate Double Bonds

notes_list.title: Ozonolysis as a Structural Tool
notes_list.basic_overview: Ozonolysis cleaves a C=C bond into carbonyl fragments, allowing the position of the original double bond to be inferred from the products.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For an unknown alkene, identify the carbonyl fragments after ozonolysis and reconnect their carbonyl carbons to reconstruct the original C=C bond. Reductive and oxidative work-ups must be distinguished.

notes_list.title: One-Carbon Shortening
notes_list.basic_overview: Hunsdiecker reaction provides a diagnostic carbon-skeleton transformation because the carboxyl carbon is removed.
notes_list.extra_info_content: If an alkyl carboxylic acid derivative gives an alkyl halide with one fewer carbon after Hunsdiecker chemistry, the lost carbon corresponds to the original carboxyl carbon.

notes_list.title: Amide to One-Carbon-Shorter Amine
notes_list.basic_overview: Hofmann bromamide rearrangement converts a primary amide into a primary amine with one fewer carbon atom.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For RCONH2, the carbonyl carbon is removed during formation and hydrolysis of the isocyanate intermediate. Therefore RCONH2 → RNH2 represents one-carbon shortening.

notes_list.title: Identify the Name Reaction from Reagents
notes_list.basic_overview: Questions may provide only reagents and ask for the reaction name or product.
notes_list.extra_info_content: High-yield reagent clues: Zn(Hg)/HCl → Clemmensen; NH2NH2/KOH/heat → Wolff–Kishner; Br2/CCl4-type conditions → alkene bromination; OsO4 → syn dihydroxylation; mCPBA → epoxidation; NBS/hν → allylic/benzylic bromination; LiAlH4 → strong reduction.

topics.title: Product Prediction
topics.basic_overview: The most common advanced questions provide a substrate and reagents and ask for the major product.
topics.extra_info_content: Solve in this order: identify reactive functional group → classify reagent as nucleophile/electrophile/oxidant/reductant/base → identify mechanism → check regioselectivity → check stereochemistry → check rearrangement possibility → draw product.

topics.title: Reaction Sequence Questions
topics.basic_overview: Multi-step synthesis questions require the output of one reaction to become the substrate of the next reaction.
topics.extra_info_content: Never treat each reagent independently. Draw the structure after every step. Then verify whether the next reagent reacts with the new functional group. This prevents many errors in multi-step GATE and CSIR-NET problems.

topics.title: Match the Following
topics.basic_overview: Reaction names, reagents, substrates and products may be given in separate columns.
topics.extra_info_content: Fast matching strategy: first identify unique signatures such as diazonium + CuCN = Sandmeyer nitrile; diazonium BF4− + heat = Balz–Schiemann; primary amide + Br2/base = Hofmann rearrangement; aldehyde + Ph3P=CHR = Wittig.

topics.title: Assertion–Reason Questions
topics.basic_overview: Assertion–reason questions test whether a mechanistic statement is correct and whether the stated reason actually explains it.
topics.extra_info_content: Separate the two tasks: first test whether the assertion is true, then independently test whether the reason is true, and finally check whether the reason explains the assertion.

notes_list.title: Carbonyl One-Liners
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldol → beta-hydroxy carbonyl/alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl; Cannizzaro → alcohol + carboxylate from non-enolizable aldehyde; Wittig → alkene; Grignard → alcohol; Clemmensen/Wolff–Kishner → hydrocarbon.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Remember the product signature rather than only the reagent. Carbonyl → alkene strongly suggests Wittig or related olefination; carbonyl → CH2 strongly suggests Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner; carbonyl + RMgX → alcohol after work-up.

notes_list.title: Aromatic One-Liners
notes_list.basic_overview: Friedel–Crafts alkylation → aryl alkyl; Friedel–Crafts acylation → aryl ketone; Reimer–Tiemann → ortho-hydroxybenzaldehyde from phenol; Kolbe–Schmitt → salicylic acid framework; Gattermann–Koch → aromatic aldehyde.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Use substrate clues: phenol + CHCl3/base → Reimer–Tiemann; sodium phenoxide + CO2 → Kolbe–Schmitt; benzene + RCOCl/AlCl3 → Friedel–Crafts acylation.

notes_list.title: Rearrangement One-Liners
notes_list.basic_overview: Beckmann → oxime to amide; Hofmann → primary amide to one-carbon-shorter amine; Curtius → acyl azide to isocyanate; Favorskii → alpha-halo ketone to rearranged acid derivative; Pinacol → vicinal diol to carbonyl compound.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Carbon-count clues are especially useful: Hofmann and Hunsdiecker involve one-carbon shortening in their characteristic transformations, whereas Arndt–Eistert homologation increases the carboxylic-acid chain by one carbon.

notes_list.title: Alkene/Alkyne Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: Hydroboration → anti-Markovnikov alcohol; oxymercuration → Markovnikov alcohol; Lindlar → cis-alkene; Na/NH3 → trans-alkene; ozonolysis → carbonyl fragments; mCPBA → epoxide.
notes_list.extra_info_content: This group is highly testable because each transformation has a distinctive regiochemical or stereochemical signature.

notes_list.title: Diazonium Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: ArN2+ + CuCl → ArCl; CuBr → ArBr; CuCN → ArCN; HBF4 followed by heat → ArF; hypophosphorous-acid-type reduction can replace diazonium by hydrogen under suitable conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Diazonium chemistry is a major aromatic synthesis hub because the diazonium group can be replaced by several different functional groups while preserving the aromatic framework.
